title: Double two reactants at once
hook: Doubling A speeds a reaction up. Doubling B speeds it up. Double both: how much faster?

knows: that more reactant usually makes a reaction faster
doesNotKnow: that the effects of different reactants multiply
that the exponents in a rate law come from experiments

misconception: Doubling two ingredients adds their separate speed-ups.
objective: The learner can say that when doubling A alone makes a reaction 2 times faster and doubling B alone makes it 4 times faster, doubling both makes it 2 × 4 = 8 times faster, because the effects multiply (rate = k[A][B]²).

claims.text: For many reactions the rate has the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where [A] and [B] are concentrations and k is a constant.
claims.source: Atkins, Physical Chemistry, ch. on rate laws; IUPAC Gold Book 'rate law (rate equation)'.

claims.text: The exponents m and n are found by experiment, not read from the balanced equation.
claims.source: Atkins, Physical Chemistry: reaction orders are experimentally determined; IUPAC Gold Book 'order of reaction'.

claims.text: In the made-up reaction, rate = k[A][B]²: doubling A alone makes the rate 2 times faster, doubling B alone 4 times faster.
claims.source: 2^1 = 2 and 2^2 = 4 (node; Demo.tsx rate(a, b) = a × b²). The reaction is invented for the lesson and labelled so on the stage.

claims.text: Doubling both A and B makes the rate 2 × 4 = 8 times faster, not 2 + 4 = 6 times.
Model: a made-up reaction with all other conditions (temperature, volume) unchanged; rates are relative to the start run.
claims.source: Stage label 'Made-up reaction. [A], [B] = amount per litre'; bars show rate relative to the start run (×1). Rate constants depend on temperature only.

recall.question: For rate = k[A][B], doubling A and tripling B (together) makes the rate…
recall.why: The effects multiply: doubling A gives ×2, tripling B gives ×3, and 2 × 3 = 6.
